name: MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.14704 [cs.AI]; also cross-listed cs.CL), submitted 20 Aug 2025; DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2508.14704; DBLP journals/corr/abs-2508-14704. No peer-reviewed venue identified as of the knowledge cutoff (preprint only). [uncertain] whether later accepted to a conference.
authors_affiliation: Ziyang Luo, Zhiqi Shen, Wenzhuo Yang (equal contribution), Zirui Zhao, Prathyusha Jwalapuram, Amrita Saha, Doyen Sahoo, Silvio Savarese, Caiming Xiong, Junnan Li. All affiliated with Salesforce AI Research.
code_url: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/MCP-Universe (official; ~588 stars, ~85 forks at time of access). Project website: https://mcp-universe.github.io
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/MCP-Universe - extensible evaluation framework with UI support, allowing community to integrate new agents and MCP servers; hosts all 231 tasks, 84 evaluators, and several in-repo MCP servers (Yahoo Finance, Blender, Google Search, Weather, Date). Project page https://mcp-universe.github.io. No persistent public leaderboard is described in the paper, though the framework is positioned as a living testbed for the evolving MCP ecosystem.
task_domain: tool-use / agentic decision-making benchmark: evaluating LLM agents that plan, select, sequence, and invoke real-world tools exposed by Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across 6 domains (Location Navigation, Repository Management, Financial Analysis, 3D Designing, Browser Automation, Web Searching). Touches web, code/repo, and embodied-design (3D) sub-domains, but is fundamentally a real tool-use / function-calling benchmark over large, unfamiliar tool spaces.
problem_setting: Interactive, multi-turn, single-agent tool-use evaluation grounded in REAL (not simulated) MCP servers connected to authentic external services (Google Maps, GitHub, Yahoo Finance, Blender, Playwright, Google Search, Fetch, plus supporting Notion/Weather/Date/Calculator servers). A task tau is a tuple (G, C, T_available): G is a natural-language goal, C is initial context/background, and T_available is the union of tools from the available MCP servers. The agent must identify, sequence, and invoke appropriate tools from T_available to achieve G given C, reasoning over partial information, adapting to diverse tool interfaces, and handling tool-response ambiguities/failures. Long-horizon multi-turn tool calling is required; input tokens grow rapidly with interaction steps (long-context challenge). The main experiments use a ReAct agent (thought-then-action loop); GPT-OSS, which cannot follow ReAct, uses the OpenAI Agent SDK instead. The benchmark is off-the-shelf evaluation of frontier LLMs (no training/supervision of the models is provided by the benchmark); temperature is set to 1.0 for all LLMs. Evaluation is execution-based and binary (pass/fail) via E: M x A x T -> {0,1}.
what_is_retrieved: tools (MCP server tool APIs). The agent must select and invoke the correct tools from the set of tools exposed by the available real-world MCP servers (133 tools across 11 servers; in the stress test 94 tools across 7 servers). There is no separate document/case/demo retrieval corpus; 'retrieval' here is real tool selection/identification within a large, partly unfamiliar tool space, plus, for Web Searching, agent-initiated web/document content fetching via the Google Search and Fetch MCP servers.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus of real tools/services. The retrievable surface is the fixed set of tools exposed by real-world MCP servers selected per task (their tool schemas/specifications and live data endpoints). It is NOT an agent-written growing/episodic memory; the agent does not persist cases or experiences across tasks. (Within Web Searching tasks, agents query live external web data, but this is task-time data access, not a self-grown memory store.)
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Not a top-k retrieval-ranking objective. The benchmark does not score Recall@k/nDCG over tools; instead the agent is given the full set of available tools per task (all schemas in context) and must select and chain the complete minimal set of correct tool calls to satisfy a multi-step goal (execution-based completeness). Success requires recovering the correct multi-tool plan, not ranking a candidate list. The 'more MCP servers connected' setting (7 servers, 94 tools) tests robustness to a larger candidate tool space rather than introducing an explicit retrieval-ranking metric.
retrieval_unit: tool-API: a single MCP tool (name + description + parameter schema) exposed by an MCP server is the unit the agent must select and invoke. Tools are grouped under servers (server -> tool hierarchy). For Web Searching, the unit additionally includes web search results and fetched URL/document content returned by the Google Search and Fetch MCP servers.
index_source: Static, offline-defined per-task tool set: for each task the framework selects the directly relevant real-world MCP servers and exposes their tools to the agent (T_available). Tool specifications come from authentic MCP servers (mostly official servers; some re-implemented over official APIs by the authors for quality). The store is fixed at task time and is not induced from the agent's own trajectories. In the stress-test variant, a larger fixed set (7 servers, 94 tools) including unrelated servers is exposed.
index_structure_topology: Hierarchical by construction: MCP servers expose sets of tools (server -> tools), formalized as S = {s_1..s_k}, each s_i exposing T_i; T_available is the union of T_i over selected servers I. Tools are presented to the agent as a flat list of tool schemas in context (no learned vector index, no dependency graph, no reranker). Topology is therefore a two-level server->tool organization surfaced as an in-context tool list. [uncertain] whether any vector/embedding index over tools is used (paper describes exposing tools directly in context, not a retriever).
retriever_type: LLM-as-selector (no dedicated retriever): the LLM agent itself selects which tool to call from the in-context tool list at each ReAct step (function-calling / tool-use). There is no BM25/dense/learned tool retriever in the standard setup; tool schemas are placed directly into the prompt and the model chooses among them. This is a key reason the benchmark exposes an 'unknown-tools' challenge.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf). The benchmark evaluates frontier LLMs as-is; no tool retriever is trained, and the models are not fine-tuned on the benchmark. Tool selection emerges from the pretrained/instruction-tuned LLM's own function-calling ability with no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signal supplied by the benchmark.
query_construction: Thought-conditioned action generation: under the ReAct framework the LLM first generates a thought based on the latest observation, then generates the next action (tool call with arguments) based on that thought. The 'query' is thus the model's self-generated tool-call decision and parameters, derived from the goal G, context C, prior observations, and the exposed tool schemas. For Web Searching, the agent additionally formulates search queries and URLs to pass to the Google Search / Fetch tools.
query_granularity: step/state-level: a tool-selection decision is made at each ReAct interaction step, conditioned on the running observation history. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0; tool choices unfold step-by-step over a long-horizon multi-turn trajectory (mean successful-task steps ~5-8 depending on model).
when_to_retrieve: iterative / agent-initiated: the agent decides at each step whether and which tool to invoke within the ReAct thought-action loop until it produces a final answer (or hits step/context limits). Tool use is interleaved across the multi-step rollout; there is no fixed retrieval schedule, learned router, or uncertainty trigger built into the benchmark.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated request governed by the ReAct loop: retrieval/tool-invocation is triggered whenever the model, in its generated action, decides a tool call is needed to make progress toward the goal. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, learned-complexity classifier, or reflection-token mechanism is imposed by the benchmark; the trigger is purely the agent emitting a tool-call action. (The optional exploration phase adds an upfront, agent-driven free-interaction stage before the exploitation/ReAct phase, but this is an analysis intervention, not the standard trigger.)
reranking: None. No reranking stage over tools or retrieved content is applied; the agent selects tools directly from the in-context list. (No cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking is described.)
retrieved_context_refinement: None by default in the main benchmark; tool outputs (observations) are fed back to the agent verbatim, which contributes to the long-context challenge. As an analysis intervention (Sec 4.3), the authors add an optional per-step Summarization Agent that compresses raw MCP server outputs to reduce context length while preserving essential information; this yields only mixed results (helps Location Navigation for GPT-4.1/Claude-4.0-Sonnet, neutral/negative for Browser Automation and Financial Analysis). Thus compression is studied as a candidate refinement but is not part of the standard pipeline.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation within an interactive agentic loop: selected tool schemas are placed in the prompt, the agent issues tool calls, the real MCP server executes them against live services, and the returned observations are appended to the context to inform subsequent thoughts/actions. Tool outputs are used directly for reasoning and final-answer construction. The benchmark itself provides no training signal; usage is purely inference-time tool invocation and grounding.
planning_integration: Per-step interleaved plan-and-act via ReAct (thought -> action -> observation, repeated). The agent implicitly plans a sequence of tool calls across a long-horizon multi-turn trajectory; there is no MCTS/tree search and no explicit plan-then-retrieve module in the standard setup. Alternative agent architectures are compared (ReAct, ReAct-with-Exploration, Cursor Agent, OpenAI Agent SDK), showing agent-framework design materially affects planning quality (e.g., o3 + OpenAI Agent SDK 31.60% vs o3 + ReAct 26.41%).
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-tool-call within a rollout (equivalently per-ReAct-step): each thought is followed by an action that may be a tool call, and retrieval/tool-use is interleaved at the granularity of individual tool invocations across the multi-step interaction trace.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured tool specifications and live execution results: tools are represented as their MCP schemas (name, description, parameters) injected into the prompt; tool outputs are returned as structured/textual observations (e.g., Google Maps place lists, Playwright HTML/page snapshots, Yahoo Finance time-series, GitHub branch/issue data). For Web Searching, search-result snippets and fetched page content (raw or, optionally, summarized) are injected. No distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable skill, or latent-token representation is used.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw tool documentation + raw live tool outputs (low abstraction). The retrievable units are concrete tool API specifications and the literal data returned by real services; there is no distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill abstraction.
noise_robustness_mechanism: None built into the benchmark; robustness to irrelevant tools is instead MEASURED. The 'More MCP Servers Connected' experiment (Sec 4.5) deliberately exposes 7 servers / 94 tools (including unrelated ones), showing consistent performance drops (e.g., Claude-4.0-Sonnet Location Navigation 22.22% -> 11.11%; GPT-4.1 Browser Automation 23.08% -> 15.38%, Financial Analysis 40.00% -> 35.00%), demonstrating brittleness to tool-space noise. The optional summarization agent (context refinement) is the only studied mitigation for noisy long outputs, and it is only partially effective.
memory_type: none. The agent has no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory that persists across tasks. Each task is solved independently; only the within-task conversation trace is retained in context.
write_back: false: the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any retrievable memory. (The optional exploration phase lets the model accumulate tool knowledge within a single task, but this is in-context and not written to a persistent store; tasks remain independent.)
online_growth: false: the retrievable tool set is fixed per task and does not grow from the agent's own outputs at test time. The framework is extensible by humans (researchers can add new MCP servers/agents), but this is offline benchmark extension, not online memory growth during agent deployment.
write_back_trigger: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and evaluators are created and cross-checked offline by the authors; no model success/failure/reflection event writes to a persistent memory at inference time.
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved as memory. The paper performs qualitative error analysis (e.g., the 'naive error' where o3 copies format requirements verbatim; the Yahoo Finance identical start/end-date error illustrating unknown-tools failures) to characterize failure modes, but does not persist failures as negative cases for retrieval or learning. The exploration phase can let a model learn correct tool usage within a task, indirectly reducing such errors, but without an explicit failure store.
memory_evolution_update: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The benchmark's task/server set is updated only by human curation and framework extension, not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: tool selection is performed by the off-the-shelf LLM via prompting/function-calling, not by an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. No M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained retrieval policy is involved.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No shared memory across agents. The benchmark is single-agent per evaluation. However, the framework is explicitly cross-FRAMEWORK at the evaluation level: it standardizes comparison of heterogeneous agent architectures (ReAct, ReAct-with-Exploration, Cursor Agent, OpenAI Agent SDK) over the same MCP servers, and is designed for the community to plug in new agents/servers. There is no shared experience/memory store between agents.
benchmarks: MCP-Universe (introduced by this paper): 231 tasks across 6 domains and 11 MCP servers with 133 total tools, evaluated by 84 unique execution-based evaluators (4 format / 32 static / 48 dynamic). Domain task counts: Web Searching 55 (23.8%), Location Navigation 45 (19.5%), Financial Analysis 40 (17.3%), Browser Automation 39 (16.9%), Repository Management 33 (14.3%), 3D Designing 19 (8.2%). Real-world MCP servers: Google Maps, GitHub, Yahoo Finance, Blender, Playwright, Google Search, Fetch, plus supporting Notion, Weather, Date, and Calculator servers.
benchmark_family: tool (real tool-use / function-calling benchmark over MCP servers). Positioned within the agent/tool-calling benchmark family alongside API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, GAIA, AppWorld, tau-Bench, and BFCLv3, and directly contrasted with contemporary MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench). Spans web (Browser Automation via Playwright, Web Searching), code/repo (GitHub), and design (Blender 3D) sub-domains, but is fundamentally a tool benchmark.
baselines: Frontier LLMs evaluated under the ReAct agent (GPT-OSS under OpenAI Agent SDK). Proprietary: GPT-5, Grok-4, Claude-4.0-Sonnet, o3, o4-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o. Open-source (>=120B): GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2, Qwen3-Coder (480B-A35B), Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, DeepSeek-V3-0324, GPT-OSS-120B. Agent-framework comparison baselines: ReAct vs Cursor Agent (Claude-4.0-Sonnet backbone) and ReAct vs OpenAI Agent SDK (o3 backbone). Comparison of MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench) on real-world integration, temporal dynamics, and execution-based evaluation (Table 1).
key_metrics: (1) Success Rate (SR, %) per domain and overall, from binary execution-based pass/fail E in {0,1}. (2) Average Evaluator score (AE, %): average percentage of evaluators passed per task (finer-grained partial credit). (3) Average Steps (AS): average number of interaction steps for successful tasks (efficiency; not available for GPT-OSS which does not follow ReAct). Also reported: success rate broken down by evaluator type (Format / Static / Dynamic). No Recall@k/nDCG, latency, or dollar-cost metrics are reported.
headline_result: Even SOTA models struggle: GPT-5 achieves the best overall success rate of 43.72% (AE 60.23%, AS 8.22), followed by Grok-4 at 33.33% and Claude-4.0-Sonnet at 29.44%. Best open-source model GLM-4.5 reaches 24.68%, surpassing some proprietary models (o4-mini 25.97% is close; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 24.24%). The low absolute ceiling (<44%) is the central headline, exposing brittleness of frontier LLM agents on real-world MCP tool use.
ablations: (1) Evaluator-type breakdown (Table 4): non-reasoning models pass >90% of Format evaluators (Claude-4.0-Sonnet 98.29%) while reasoning models do worse on format (Gemini-2.5-Flash 51.28%, o3 73.50%); the large gap between Format (often >80%) and Static/Dynamic content evaluators (~40-66%) shows failures stem mainly from content generation, not format. GPT-5 leads Static (61.92%, tied with Claude-4.0-Sonnet) and Dynamic (65.96%). (2) Long-context analysis (Fig 4): tokens grow rapidly with interaction steps (measured on Claude-4.0-Sonnet); adding a per-step Summarization Agent gives mixed results (helps Location Navigation for GPT-4.1/Claude-4.0-Sonnet, neutral/negative elsewhere). (3) Unknown-tools analysis (Fig 5): adding an Exploration phase before exploitation improves some domains (GPT-4.1 Browser Automation +7.69pp to 30.77%; Claude-4.0-Sonnet Financial Analysis +7.50pp to 62.50%) but is not universally beneficial (Claude-4.0-Sonnet Browser Automation declines; GPT-4.1 Financial Analysis flat). (4) More servers connected (Fig 6): exposing 7 servers/94 tools (incl. unrelated) degrades performance (e.g., Claude-4.0-Sonnet Location Navigation 22.22% -> 11.11%). (5) Agent-framework comparison (Table 5): ReAct (29.44%) > Cursor Agent (26.41%) on Claude-4.0-Sonnet; OpenAI Agent SDK (31.60%) > ReAct (26.41%) on o3, with o3+Agent SDK the best agent-backbone combo.
evaluation_decoupling: Partial / not in the retrieval sense. The benchmark does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (no Recall@k/nDCG over tools). It does, however, decouple evaluation along orthogonal axes: per-domain success rates, evaluator-type breakdown (Format vs Static vs Dynamic), an Average Evaluator (AE) score giving partial credit on sub-criteria distinct from binary task success, and Average Steps (AS) for efficiency. Tool-selection competence surfaces indirectly through these and through the unknown-tools / more-servers analyses rather than via standalone retrieval metrics.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both. Outcome: binary task Success Rate. Process/intermediate: Average Evaluator (AE) score (fraction of per-task sub-criteria/evaluators satisfied), Average Steps (AS) for successful tasks (trajectory efficiency), Format/Static/Dynamic evaluator breakdown localizing where failure occurs (format compliance vs content correctness vs temporal correctness), and qualitative error analyses (naive format-copying error; unknown-tools parameter misuse) that diagnose process-level failures.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Reported via Average Steps (AS) and the long-context analysis rather than dollar/latency. AS for successful tasks: o3 most efficient among top models at 4.82 steps despite 26.41% SR; GPT-5 8.22 steps, Grok-4 7.75, Gemini-2.5-Flash 8.26; open-source mostly 5-7 (DeepSeek-V3 most efficient at 5.06). The benchmark emphasizes the long-context cost: input tokens grow rapidly with steps (measured on Claude-4.0-Sonnet), often causing context overflow; a summarization agent reduces context but gives mixed accuracy effects. No explicit API-cost, wall-clock latency, or token-count-per-task tables are provided.
context_budget_and_selection_count: No fixed token budget or fixed-k tool count is set per query; all available tools' schemas are placed in context (133 tools in the standard relevant-server setup; 94 tools in the 7-server stress test), and tool outputs accumulate. This produces a growing, unbounded context that the paper identifies as the long-context challenge (tokens increase rapidly with interaction steps, risking context overflow). The optional per-step summarization agent is the only budget-management mechanism studied, and it is not part of the default protocol.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Size: 231 tasks; 6 domains; 11 MCP servers; 133 tools; 84 unique execution-based evaluators (4 Format, 32 Static, 48 Dynamic). Construction: tasks are MANUALLY designed by the authors to reflect real use cases, with 4-5 sub-task types per domain (e.g., route planning/optimal stops/location/place finding for navigation; portfolio analysis/financial statements/trading strategies/institutional holdings/dividend analysis for finance); a task is rejected as too easy if it can be solved without MCP servers or consistently solved within five retries, prompting brainstorming of a harder one; every task and evaluator is cross-checked by other authors for feasibility, ambiguity, and correctness. Answer verifiability: HIGH and execution-based (not LLM-as-judge) - Format evaluators check strict output formatting, Static evaluators check time-invariant ground truth (manually collected, e.g., historical stock prices, exact goal counts), and Dynamic evaluators automatically fetch real-time ground truth (e.g., live flight prices, current weather, current GitHub issue counts) via tool calls for stable evaluation across timestamps. Difficulty signal: best system GPT-5 reaches only 43.72% overall SR, with several domains (Location Navigation, Repository Management) far lower, indicating high real-world difficulty and an unknown-tools / long-context challenge.
builds_on: MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic (late 2024), as the integration standard (JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO/SSE; host/client/server three-layer architecture). The ReAct agent framework (Yao et al., 2023) as the primary agent pipeline; also evaluates ReAct-with-Exploration, the OpenAI Agent SDK, and the Cursor Agent. Uses real official/community MCP servers (Google Maps, GitHub, Playwright, Fetch, Notion, Calculator) and authors' own API-backed servers (Yahoo Finance, Blender, Google Search, Weather, Date). Conceptually builds on the agent/tool-use evaluation lineage (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, GAIA, AppWorld, tau-Bench, BFCLv3).
contrasts_with: Contemporary MCP benchmarks (Table 1): MCPWorld (real-world + exec-eval but GUI-heavy, no temporal dynamics), MCP-RADAR (derivative of HumanEval/GSM8k, not real-world, no temporal dynamics, though exec-based), MCPEval and LiveMCPBench (both rely on LLM-as-a-Judge, unsuitable for real-time tasks and prone to style bias; LiveMCPBench is real-world+temporal but not exec-based). MCP-Universe is the only one combining real-world integration, temporal dynamics, AND execution-based evaluation. Also contrasted with simplistic prior benchmarks focused on isolated abilities (instruction following, math reasoning, function calling) and with enterprise agents (Cursor) which it shows do not beat plain ReAct.
lineage: Group E (tool-use): a real-world tool-use BENCHMARK for the MCP era. It extends the function-calling/tool benchmark lineage (API-Bank -> ToolBench/ToolLLM -> GAIA/AppWorld/tau-Bench/BFCLv3) into execution-based evaluation over authentic MCP servers with temporal (real-time ground-truth) dynamics, and sits among 2025 MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench). It exposes brittleness in real tool selection over large/unfamiliar tool spaces (the 'unknown-tools' and long-context challenges), serving as a difficulty-defining testbed rather than a retrieval method.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: partial (the agent selects/identifies the right tools from the available MCP tool set, but this is tool selection, not retrieval of prior solved cases), Reuse: no, Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a real-world MCP tool-use benchmark with execution-based evaluation.
tool_document_engineering: Minimal / raw: tools are exposed using their native MCP schemas (name, description, parameter spec) directly in the agent context; the paper does not apply synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings. The 'unknown-tools' challenge is precisely that raw MCP tool docs are often insufficient for correct usage (e.g., Yahoo Finance requiring distinct start/end dates), motivating the optional exploration phase as a remedy rather than offline document engineering.
index_content_separation: Limited: in the standard setup all available tool schemas and their (potentially large) outputs are loaded into context, with no separation of a lightweight index from heavy content - a deliberate stressor producing the long-context challenge. The optional per-step Summarization Agent partially separates essential information from raw heavy tool outputs (a form of on-demand content compression), but it is an analysis intervention, not a default progressive-disclosure / index-then-content design.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: MCP-based, live tool index over REAL servers: tools are accessed through the Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO/SSE) against authentic API endpoints with real authentication, so tool outputs reflect live, temporally changing data (handled by dynamic evaluators that fetch real-time ground truth). The framework dynamically configures which servers/tools are exposed per task and is extensible to new servers (researchers can add servers), but it does not perform automatic CRUD live-sync of a tool catalog at agent runtime; the per-task tool set is fixed once configured.
tool_dependency_awareness: Not explicitly modeled by any retrieval/ranking component; inter-tool dependencies are left to the LLM agent to infer. Tasks inherently require multi-tool chaining where one tool's output feeds another (e.g., GitHub: list branches -> create/copy file -> open PR; Finance: fetch institutional-holdings date -> convert to calendar date -> pull closing price for that day; Navigation: compute route polyline -> search place near midpoint -> validate place type). The benchmark thus tests dependency-aware planning, but provides no dependency graph or dependency-aware reranker; correct sequencing is the agent's responsibility.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR). The closest analogue is that the agent reads each tool's schema and live outputs and instantiates correctly-formatted, correctly-sequenced tool calls (parameter slot-filling and chaining grounded in the tool docs and observations), optionally informed by a prior exploration phase, rather than adapting a retrieved prior solution case.
